title: Drying as Heat and Mass Transfer

content.overview: Drying is a product process, not merely a room setpoint. Heat and water move through flowers and surrounding air at rates shaped by material structure, load arrangement and environmental distribution.

vocabulary.definition: Movement of water from wetter material toward drier air or material regions.
Air region near a material surface that can influence heat and moisture transfer.
Difference in moisture condition across a flower, container, rack or room.

sections.title: Coupled variables shape drying rate
sections.body: Temperature, humidity, airflow, flower geometry and loading interact. Changing one variable can alter both water removal and quality outcomes.

sections.title: Material is not spatially uniform
sections.body: Outer tissue can dry sooner than internal or sheltered material, and dense or poorly exposed zones can follow a different trajectory from the room average.

sections.title: Process choices create tradeoffs
sections.body: Cannabis and hemp studies show that drying conditions can change duration, volatiles, color, microbial outcomes and cannabinoid chemistry. Treatment-specific findings are evidence of tradeoffs, not universal recipes.

workedExamples: Two racks share the same room trend but differ in loading and airflow exposure; equal room conditions do not prove equal product condition.
commonMistakes: Treating room relative humidity as the product endpoint.
Assuming all flower sizes dry at the same rate.
Copying a research treatment as a universal facility setpoint.
content.practicalApplication: Draw the material and airflow path for a drying load and identify where representative product measurements are needed to detect gradients.
content.summary: Drying control requires product evidence across meaningful locations because room conditions, material properties and airflow jointly determine the result.
